utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Court Deputy, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand that before we hear the witness the Defence has something to raise at this stage. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. Well, there's two matters actually. The first one is that in court today is an individual that I'm not familiar with. He's seated at the back there. My instructions are that's a man by the name of Mr. Fahrija Karkin who is, as we understand it, associated in some way with Mr. Delalic. We no basis for him being in Court whatsoever. We seek some guidance from the Prosecutors as to why he should be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. The Prosecution has been pre-empted in this. I was going to introduce Mr. Fahrija Karkin. He is Ramiz Delalic's lawyer. I have sought permission from Your Honours to have him sit in court behind the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this request should be granted and Mr. Fahrija Karkin, would you please introduce yourself for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARKIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Fahrija Karkin and I am an attorney from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I wasn't aware of the -- of the learned Prosecutor approaching the Court and seeking this permission for this person to be in court. Your Honours, it should be clarified so that the Defence understands what the role of this -- of Mr. Karkin is here and it should be clarified by the Prosecutors as to what role he is going to play in these proceedings and why it is that they have asked and sought permission for him to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, Mr. Karkin accompanied Mr. Ramiz Delalic from Sarajevo here. He asked for permission to be accompanied, Mr. Ramiz Delalic by his lawyer, and this permission was granted and he accompanied him and he is asking as Mr. Ramiz Delalic's lawyer in all aspects. In respect to what he is going to be doing in court, he is going to be listening, I don't think there's going to be any other input into the proceedings whatsoever, and Mr. Delalic will be giving his evidence and his lawyer would be present in case there would be any questions of self-incrimination that he would like his lawyer's advice on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that is the normal practice of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have to say we'll have to see how things develop in that regard, but there is some chance that he would end up being a witness. So it's a matter for the Prosecutors, frankly, and for this Tribunal. But based upon what's been led there, the Defence does not -- in any event, I take it Your Honours have issued a ruling about this. I'm not going to seek to canvass that. I've raised what I've got to raise, but I'm going to concede it could cause trouble in the future and when the questions begin that will be apparent. Your Honour's, the next thing I have to raise is the proofing notes that we've received concerning Mr. Delalic. Now, in this trial the pleadings have made it clear -- the indictment's made it clear and the various briefs that have been issued since that time that what Mr. Halilovic has faced up until today is a case as to -- failure to punish the crime at Grabovica. It's been said that he didn't do enough, effectively. It's been said that upon learning of the crime, he reacted inadequately is, I think, the short way of putting the Prosecution case. Now, with the second-last witness in the trial or the third-last witness depending on the expert, Your Honours it appears Mr. Halilovic was in a conspiracy to murder Rasim Delic, that there was a long-standing plan to do this, to have put back in charge of the army. And apparently it's now said by this witness that at all times there was a contingency plan for this witness who's coming along now to kill Delic, if necessary, which this witness offered to do, and that operation Neretva seems to be one step in the campaign of Mr. Halilovic to be returned to his position, according to this set of proofing notes, as head of the army. Now, those allegations are way outside the indictment that we face and they place the Defence in a very unusual position. We haven't dealt with these allegations with witnesses who have come. If we knew we were going to meet an allegation that there was a plan to kill -- which is the allegation here, that there was a plan to kill Rasim Delic, if needs be, and return Halilovic to the head of the army that way, then there are many questions one might have asked many witnesses on that topic. Now, we note that there is a reason now at this time, we note that it is not in the pleadings, we note that it places the Defence in a very unusual position of having to either deal with it on the run, which I want to say in advance we are going to cross-examine this witness and we are not going to seek any delays or adjournments now; he's here, and we are going to deal with him. But it places the Defence in a position where we have let witnesses go by who may have been able to comment on this issue because it wasn't raised. And it throws into very sharp relief a problem that I've raised before, and that's this one: What parts of this witness's evidence does the Prosecution rely on? Because it's there case as pleaded in their indictment and as repeated by Ms. Chana at a pre-trial -- at a conference recently that Ramiz Delalic was the commander of these troops, despite his denial of that, and that Ramiz Delalic ordered the burial of bodies. Now, it's not for me to issue attacks on Ramiz Delalic before his evidence begins; I'll cross-examine him in due course. But the Prosecution themselves say that. Now the Defence is in the position where we don't know precisely what parts of this man's evidence the Prosecutor are asking you to believe and which parts they're asking you to disbelieve. It's a trial by ambush and it puts the Defence in the position where they have to decide what to deal with, what allegations to deal with. Do we call -- do we attack this man on materials which the Prosecution do not seek to prove? Is the Prosecution prepared to lead evidence from a witness that they know and they assert is untrue? Now, Your Honours, the reason I raise it now is because -- it's for the final time before this witness gives his evidence. We call on the Prosecutor to say, now, you the Tribunal are entitled to know, and the Defence must be able to know which parts of this witness's evidence the Prosecution say can be believed and do they rely on, and in which particulars is this witness lying, as the Prosecution says he is, as they must be saying he is because that's what their indictment says and that's what they say in the pre-trial materials. So we now call on the Prosecutors to indicate now clearly, as they should, so that we can know how to deal with this witness. In what particulars is he telling the truth and in what particulars is he lying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, it is the first time for me to hear that there is a conspiracy to murder Mr. Delic participated in or organised by Mr. Halilovic. So I believe at this stage we also need an explanation from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This transpired at the proofing notes, Your Honour -- at the time of proofing and I diligently wrote down everything which was new, as I'm obliged to do, which the witness had told me in proofing. And this particular topic, Your Honour, arose when we were discussing the closeness of his relationship with the accused in this case. Your Honour, the pleadings have not changed, the indictment has not changed. This goes towards showing the relationship that the accused had with Mr. Halilovic. And this is what the witness said and I wrote it down and I handed it over to the Defence. Your Honour, it is not for the Defence to ask us before the witness has given evidence as to what portions of his evidence that we rely upon. He hasn't given his evidence yet; these are proofing notes. Once Mr. Delalic has given evidence, the Defence will then be in a position to request from us at such time as the closing briefs or at the 98 bis stage, in which we will address as to what parts of any witness's evidence we rely on. We have not -- we have not changed the pleadings, we are charging Mr. Halilovic with conspiracy to murder. This all goes towards the relationship of the accused and Operation Neretva. How is it that it came to pass that this operation was conceived? These are all very relevant issues to the case at hand and when the witness comes and gives his evidence it will become very obvious in the context that this piece of evidence will be used. Quite frankly, Your Honour, the Prosecution finds this submissions pre-emptive to the issue. It's quite a case of damned if you do, damned if you don't. If I had not noted that in the proofing notes, I would not have done my obligation to the Defence to note down everything and hand it over to the Defence as to what the accused had said. I mean, I'm sorry, the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but as a rule, Ms. Chana, the evidence you will lead from this witness should be strictly within the scope of the indictment. Here I believe that we are going to address whether Mr. Halilovic is responsible for the Grabovica and Uzdol incidents or massacres rather than something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and part of the Prosecution theory has always been that he brought these troops on to the field in Herzegovina and this witness is giving another explanation as to why these troops were brought in to Herzegovina. It's part of the Prosecution theory, and this is something which was stated in our pre-trial brief, in the opening statement, that these troops were specifically chosen by Mr. Halilovic. The Defence in their pre-trial brief have actually rebutted this issue and said, no, it was not Halilovic who brought these troops on into Herzegovina. It all goes towards that Prosecution theory. Your Honour, I'm advised by Your Honours and I will of course confine my examination-in-chief to the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. And we also would like to thank the Defence for reminding us of this point and we'll hear the testimony of this witness -- and as for how much weight we should attach to his testimony is a matter that the Bench will consider at a later stage. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Well, before we start, I believe it is my duty to remind you of the Rule 90(E), which says: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than forced testimony." Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please state your name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of February, 1963. My name is Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I do have a nickname. Since my childhood they've called me Celo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where were you born, Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I was born in the Republic of Serbia, in Priboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was there a time that you moved to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you remember what year that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I seek permission from the Court to lead this witness on his criminal background?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, before the war, were you charged for theft but you were acquitted in 1989?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1990 there were charges against you for attempted double murder and you were again acquitted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In October 1993 you were charged with various offences in one indictment, such as using fire weapons in public places and jeopardising the safety of civilians, acts of extortion of money, et cetera. You were --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- acquitted for all charges except for refusal to carry out an order --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- and you were sentenced to three years.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you were in custody for seven and a half months?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were pardoned by political decree as there were --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for such acts?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I've gone out of chronology. Excuse me for that. In 2000 you were charged with assault on an unauthorised official and you were sentenced to six months imprisonment, which you served?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 2004 you were charged with violent behaviour in public and were sentenced to six months imprisonment which you completed and you were released on 28th February, 2005?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You have -- you are currently charged with murder --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- committed in 1991 and you are out on bail?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What are the conditions of your bail?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The terms of my bail are of a monetary nature, amount to 360.000 convertible marks, Bosnian marks, and I cannot have a passport. But I am on provisional release where I'm mounting my defence. I was held responsible for this murder already in 1996 when the investigative judge and the prosecutor did not pursue further charges. This indictment was re-activated once more in 2001 or 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you have been given special permission to travel to The Hague to give your testimony and your passport has been issued to you for that purpose. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Delalic. Now, can I ask you about the JNA. Did you ever serve military service in the JNA -- did you do military service, sorry, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served my military term in Tuzla in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you complete your military service?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I was in the infantry. The training lasted for six months. After training, about a month and a half later, I had surgery. I had to have my appendix out and I was temporarily released from the military for a period of four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: After four years I went for tests again, and the military commission discharged me absolutely from the military. So I no longer had to complete my military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, let's go to before the war and before the formation of the Bosnian army. What was your role in the defence of Sarajevo, if any?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war or actually a few months before the war the Green Berets were already in existence and I was a member of that group. When the war broke out on the 6th of April, 1992, I happened to be in the Bosna unit where there were -- members of who were Green Beret, Bosna 30 where I was commander of that unit. The unit numbered 30 men, the commander was Sakib Puskar and I was the deputy commander or komandir, however you want to term it. This lasted for several months then I took over the commander of the police for the municipality of Stari Grad, that is a municipality in Sarajevo. After a few months in that post, by a decision of the Presidency and the Supreme Command, I became the commander of the 3rd Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, before we go to that can you tell us what was your role as the deputy commander of this Bosna 31 unit. What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: For the most part, most units in Sarajevo were not large units, these were small units of a maximum of 30 to 40 men. Our function was to defend Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When were the front lines in Sarajevo established?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Right at the start of the war I think, but these were not properly established lines. Only about a month after the war broke out the lines were fortified.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when was the first attack on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what exactly were you -- was your duties in respect? Was it defensive? Was it attack? Can you explain a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It was mostly defence. We really didn't carry out any attacks. We didn't have anything to attack with.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you become part of the military police for a while, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know that I was transferred to that duty sometime in June or July 1992, and I remained there very briefly for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then you said you became commander of the 3rd Mountain Brigade. How long did that last for?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Also for a few months, since the supreme command and the corps command wanted to make the units larger. The supreme command ordered that the two brigades, the 3rd Mountain and another brigade be joined into the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, do you know when the 9th Motorised Brigade was formed, when the 3rd Mountain Brigade and the 7th Mountain Brigade was merged?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I think that it was sometime at the beginning of 1993 or in late 1992. But I think it was in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how many men did this brigade then have, when it merged?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade numbered approximately 5.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you said you became the deputy commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I proposed that myself. Since I didn't have a lot of military training and the brigade did number 5.000 men, I suggested that I be appointed deputy commander and Sulejman Imjirevic be appointed the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who did you suggest that to, that you should be appointed deputy commander and not the commander?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: To the corps commander, Vahid Karavelic, who really was quite happy to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why was he happy to hear that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time all the commanders were just regular men who had no particular training for commanders of brigades who had no training in carrying out military operations. And in order to lead a brigade you needed a trained person. So the plan was to let the military personnel who used to be members of the former JNA lead the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Sefer Halilovic the chief of the army at that time when the 9th Motorised Brigade was formed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was his view on the matter that you become the deputy commander and not the commander?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, he wanted me to be in the command post; however, that was difficult to implement because, as I've told you already, I wasn't properly trained for that role.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why did Sefer Halilovic want you to be in the command post? What was his reasons, stated reasons, to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, first of all the decision on appointment of the brigade commanders is not made by Sefer Halilovic, it is made by the Presidency. However, the Supreme Command plays the main role in that process. Why is it that he wanted me to be in the command post? I think that he wanted to have somebody that would support him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when you say "support," can you please elaborate. What kind of support would that be?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, among the former JNA officers, there was a lot of turmoil. In instances where the brigades had several units and several commanders, it was easier for brigade commanders to keep their function.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you a little bit about the military structures in Sarajevo in early 1993. Can you tell us a bit about the hierarchy in Bosnia-Herzegovina generally in the military. What was it like? What was the -- from the Supreme Command, the Presidency, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the president of the Presidency, so there was the Presidency, headed by the president. And following that was the chief of the Main Staff, which was the post of Sefer Halilovic; and then followed his deputies; and then the corps; and then the brigades; and then so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which was the corps under which the 9th Brigade fell in Sarajevo? Who -- which corps was in charge of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the BH Army, commanded by Vahid Karavelic. The 9th Motorised Brigade was a part of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you touched upon this a little earlier. Can you tell us the kind of commanders there were at the beginning? How would you categorise the different kinds of commanders in the Bosnian army at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, there was quite a lot of animosity among the commanders who were ordinary people -- or rather, between them and the former officers. Most of the former JNA officers transferred to the BH Army immediately after the war broke out or up to two months after that. And there was a lot of animosity between them and the ordinary commanders because those who were the former JNA members actually took part in attacking Sarajevo before they transferred to the BH Army. In addition to that, there was a lot of mistrust among the former JNA officers and the commanders who were ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How would you characterise yourself? What kind of a commander were you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I was a man of the people; that's the type of commander I was. In addition to that, I did not get along well with the commanders who used to be members of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was -- what kind of a commander was Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: We considered Sefer to be a positive figure because several months before the war he had left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you follow orders from commanders that you did not respect?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I would follow all of the orders that pertained to the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and most of the other orders, especially the orders issued by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How many battalions did the 9th Brigade have?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade had four combat battalions, one logistics battalion, and several staff units.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was the area of responsibility and your brigade's principal tasks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 9th Motorised Brigade covered almost the entire right bank of Sarajevo. Our tasks were to defend that area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I'll show you a document about that in a minute, but before we get to that I would like to ask you: How well equipped was the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade, as compared to the other brigades, was very well equipped. Approximately 65 to 70 per cent of the personnel were armed. This is in comparison to other brigades where only 25 to 30 per cent of the personnel was equipped. In my brigade, that percentage was 65 to 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how is it that you were so much better equipped than other brigades?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo there were many barracks which used to belong to the former JNA. We received a lot of weapons from there, more than other brigades, and in addition to that we also received money from the chief of the Main Staff, Sefer Halilovic, in order to purchase weapons. We had special channels for procuring weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before we get to those channels, how did you get money from Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: We received it on several occasions. We received money from Sefer Halilovic, or rather from him chef de cabinet. On several occasions we would receive 50.000 to 100.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why was it that you were given more money and more equipment? Why were you chosen, your particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the moment the witness hasn't said that he received more money than other brigades at all. He's just said that his brigade was better equipped and there shouldn't be any leading on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that's just a little bit leading, but -- well, since you object, yes, maybe you could put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How do you know that the 9th Brigade was better equipped than other brigades?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: We had almost daily meetings at the corps where the brigade commanders briefed the corps commander. When the brigade commanders reported or briefed the corps commander, each brigade commander had to report on the status within his brigade. So they would start by giving the number of personnel, the level of their equipment, the number of weapons at the disposal of that brigade and so on. Therefore, I knew that in comparison to those brigades, my brigade was much better equipped with weapons. And, in fact, my brigade was probably one of the best equipped and best armed brigades in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why is that, Mr. Delalic? Why was your brigade the best equipped in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: As I've just told you, the -- there was a lot of turmoil among the former JNA officers. They were career officers and they were very ambitious and there was always a lot of contention among them, who would climb to a higher post, who would become the commander of the staff and so on. They were less interested in the defence of Sarajevo and more in their own career. And the officer who had more commanders around him could ensure a better position for himself. This is why they were given money and arms from the -- Sefer Halilovic -- from Sefer Halilovic. It wasn't only my brigade who received that; it was also the Delta Unit, and the 10th Mountain Brigade, and the 1st Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, these other brigades, were they as well equipped as yours, Delta, the 10th Mountain Brigade, and the 1st Mountain Brigade? In comparison -- I mean, you said they were better equipped than the others, but in comparison to the 9th?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So were these other three brigades as well equipped as the 9th Brigade -- the 10th Mountain Brigade, let's begin with the 10th Mountain Brigade, how was that vis-a-vis the 9th?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not as equipped as the 9th Brigade, but compared to other brigades they were. The 10th Mountain Brigade did not have as many soldiers as the 9th Brigade, Delta also did not have as many soldiers. But percentage-wise compared to other units, they were better equipped and they had more weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How else did you finance your brigade in terms of weapons and guns and ammunition? Where else did the finance come from, if indeed it came from anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo there were a lot of shops which continued operating, cafes, taverns, and so on. There was some business activity. So the brigade collected money from voluntary contributions and through other channels. As there was an embargo imposed on Bosnia and Herzegovina, we had to find some channels and some channels went through the Croats, some went through the Serbs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were you authorised to collect money from these cafes and other businesses? Was it official?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Listen, those were mostly voluntary donations, contributions. In some cases a soldier who had just come back from the front, in order to prevent such people from creating problems, the owners of these businesses would come on their own free will and give voluntary contributions. These people did not serve in the army, and this is what irritated the soldiers, although some of the civilians did have work obligations. But soldiers were irritated by the fact that they didn't have to go and fight. And this is why problems would erupt. So mostly the money was given on a voluntary basis. However, later on as a lot of warehouses and shops were looted in Sarajevo as well as factories where there were certain goods, by way of decree of the Presidency and the Supreme Command, it was ordered that each commander in his own area of responsibility must find those goods and store them in their own warehouses. These goods were later to be distributed within the corps or within the brigade. This was another mechanism for obtaining financial funds for brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was the military background of the men who was in the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Let us start with the 3rd Mountain Brigade. The situation was quite poor in that regard. In the 7th Motorised Brigade, the situation was better.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where were they recruited from, the soldiers which came into the 9th Brigade mostly? I mean, how were they recruited?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Most of these soldiers who were members of the 9th Motorised Brigade -- I actually made a mistake. I said "the 7th Motorised Brigade," but I should have said the 9th Motorised Brigade. So most of them were recruited through military centres of the military department. That means that initially at the beginning -- in the beginning of the war, we had some volunteers but not many of them. The percentage was very low. Later on the process went through military departments, that means that it went through regular channels. However, we should also point out that -- how should I put it? The best and the most honest recruits would be sent to police, whereas the drudges or those who were not good for anything else would be sent to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Drudges, can you elaborate for Their Honours what drudges means?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, in the course of the recruitment process the best soldiers would definitely go to police and to some better brigades, staff brigades. And everybody else, the scum, all other recruits who were scum, and scum means they were no good, that they had a tendency to commit criminal offences, all of them were sent to other brigades. However, all of this was done in a regular procedure through the military department, military centres, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was the ethnic mix of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It was multi-ethnic. That means in my brigade most of the members were Bosniak Muslims. Then there were Croats, the Roma, and quite a lot of Serbs, about 100 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what impact did the break-out of the war have on the ethnic mix in the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It did not have a particular impact, a specific impact, because traditionally in Sarajevo the people led a multi-ethnic existence. That was their style of life. Although there were members of the SDS who had a different view, and many of the SDS party members remained living in Sarajevo and were protected in a way. However, the members of the 9th Motorised Brigade were not really burdened with nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What kind of training was given to your troops, if any?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: There never was any training, at least not within my brigade. If there was some training, then it was conducted by some foreign services, and I know nothing about that. For example, the training of the battalion commanders, company commanders, was nonexistent. The command of the 9th Motorised Brigade appointed people to the post based on their own opinion as to how able they were; however, there was no particular training, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what primarily were the duties? Was it more defensive or assault the 9th Brigade undertook?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The tasks of the 9th Motorised Brigade were mostly of the defensive nature, not of the offensive, although we did conduct some attacks; however, that was very rarely and those were operations of a very limited nature in terms of length, including a very small number of personnel. That means that most of us commanders who were men of the people were against conducting any larger offensive operation because we knew we had no capabilities for that. And this was another reason for disagreement among us who were not members of the former JNA and those who used to be members of the former JNA. We mostly were of the opinion that we needed to defend Sarajevo, whereas they believed that we needed to conduct a large offensive which would mean that a lot of people were killed or were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did each unit have within it an assault detachment?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Each brigade, even each battalion, had to have its sabotage unit. When I talked about the composition of the 9th Motorised Brigade, I told you that it had four battalions, combat battalions, and logistics units. And in accordance with its structure, each battalion, each brigade had to have assault units, engineering units, demining units, and so on. That means that each brigade had to have within its composition several sabotage units and several assault units. In addition to that, by order of the corps commander, Vahid Karavelic, the commanders were required to always have at their disposal one unit numbering about 100 men who would be able at any time to come to the aid of another brigade, because very often we would have situations where one brigade was exposed to a very severe enemy attack, so all other brigades had to come to the aid of that brigade, all other brigades which were deployed in other areas but had to have light units, well equipped, who could get to another part very easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how would it be decided who would go into action, which units would go into action when the circumstances which you just described arose?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: As for the 9th Motorised Brigade, the brigade within its composition had a sabotage or assault detachment and each battalion had to have a sabotage platoon, which means up to 30 people. And then the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade would select the most capable people for that task or for that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to now show you a document, and you will be assisted by the court usher, which is D402. Is it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what is this? Can you just tell us what this map is of?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: This map depicts the areas of responsibility of each brigade in Sarajevo. The 1st Mountain Brigade, the 2nd Mountain Brigade, the 9th Motorised Brigade, the 1st Motorised Brigade, 2nd Motorised Brigade, and so on. So this map depicts the area of responsibility of the 9th Motorised Brigade, but I think that the area depicted here is much smaller than it was in reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So would you say it's not drawn to scale? Obviously it's not drawn to scale; it's been done by hand. No criticism to anyone who drew it. What percentage of the front line was the 9th Brigade holding?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It had the largest area of responsibility. I couldn't really give you the exact percentage, but when I say to you that it was responsible for the entire right flank or part of Sarajevo, I mean the nucleus of the city, and that was defended by the 9th Motorised Brigade. Now, as to the percentage, it would be 20 to 25 per cent. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Other than that, is this an accurate description of the various brigades and their area of responsibility? Does this map accurately depict the various brigades and the front line of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It's more or less like that. This was sketched in hand, so perhaps it's not so precise. As far as my own 9th Motorised Brigade, it seems that the area depicted here is a little bit smaller than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, Mr. Delalic, what was the reputation of the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Because of their attachment - how shall I put it? - to the Chief of the Main Staff, Sefer Halilovic, most of the services in Sarajevo wanted to represent the 9th Motorised Brigade as a criminal element. However, I don't believe myself that that was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So how -- what, according to you, was the truth about the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by the things that happened in Sarajevo, and that means various criminal acts that happened, not only in my brigade but in other brigades, but a commander - and I'm not only speaking about myself - but a brigade commander could not have everything under control, each fighter under his control, especially not in the 9th Motorised Brigade. The commander or the command could not have control over every fighter. My brigade numbered almost 5.000 people, and they all had to be monitored. But judging by the things that happened in the other brigades, for example, the 10th Mountain Brigade where there were a lot of crimes against civilians, or the 2nd Viteska or Knightly [Realtime transcript read in error, "9th"] Brigade which was given that name because it was one of the best brigades. There were a lot of crimes and killings of civilians. Then we can also look at the 5th Motorised Brigade. People were also taken for digging and then they disappeared and so on and so forth. In all the brigades, there were crimes against civilians. In my brigade, there wasn't a single crime against civilians during the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there any other criminality --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt for one moment there. I apologise, but there's a possible typographical error here, Your Honours, at line 22. What it says is that the -- the witness said "but a commander, I'm not only speaking about myself, but a brigade commander could not have everything under control, each fighter under his control." He went on to say, especially -- sorry, no, I've jumped too early. If you go down to line -- page 25, line 1, you'll see there it says: "Judging by the things that happened in the other brigades, for example, the 10th Mountain Brigade or where there was a lot of crime against civilians. Or the 2nd Viteska or 9th Brigade. " It says "9th Brigade" there. I think the witness said "Knightly Brigade," and it's been translated as "9th." But that should be clarified because I think it's contrary to what the witness's intention was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, maybe you could clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Delalic, you heard the Defence counsel. Did you mean to say the 9th Brigade or the Knightly Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade. The other Viteska Brigade that I talked about, which was considered to be one of the most honest and the best brigades according to the criteria of the Presidency in the 2nd Corps, that brigade actually committed a lot of -- or the soldiers of that brigade committed a lot of crimes against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the 9th Brigade. What kind of criminality was present there, if any, according to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Of course, just like in any other brigades, soldiers got their hands on different kinds of narcotics, mostly alcohol. Soldiers would have the habit of getting drunk and maybe committing something in that state, but all of these incidents were recorded. But for certain there were no killings of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now, were you aware that MUP was writing reports about yourself and your brigade and casting your brigade in a negative light?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to see one such report, please, and I ask the court usher if they would please put on 65 ter number 153 and the number is 0218-3117.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 415.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That document will come up on your screen. You had occasion to see this document during our proofing session. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, within this document there are various allegations made against your brigade, and I show you this one by way of example. There are others, as you know. Now, I'll just highlight some of the things which are -- which were said about you and your brigade. "Illegal and unruly actions of Ramiz Delalic have been circulated for quite some time amongst the 9th Motorised Brigade's troops," and they talk about the period of August 1992 and April 1993. "Troops of the aforementioned brigade took away cattle that belonged to civilians," then you have "illegal requisition of civilians' property while searching apartments and business premises," and then there is "estranging the inventory and property of many state-owned and private premises," so basically a lot of theft. You were, "obtained operative intelligence suggests that Delalic usurped a number of luxury apartments in the central part of the city." You've -- there's allegations of stealing a Honda car. There's allegations of physically abusing members of the aforementioned brigades as well as members of other units of the ARBiH, the allegations of assaulting one member of the ARBiH. You carried out or is alleged carried out operations in collaboration with the Chetniks who shelled the HVO positions after Delalic gave them coordinates. You organised the wearing of badges with Sefer Halilovic's picture, which had to be worn by all members of the 9th Motorised Brigade. And various amounts of money, extortion, to purchase guns and ammunition. And of course it ends up talking about the massacres committed against the Croatian civilians in the battlefields of Herzegovina and the various crimes and the killings there. Now, I would like to now give you an opportunity to tell me what you -- how -- what do you say about documents such as this?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you to remind me later about this crime against the Croatian population because I would like to say something about that. But I would like to say something else first about these things that you talked before that. This note indicates that these various services that were active in Sarajevo were actually busying themselves with silly things and were busier with who stole what from some apartment rather than those -- with those who killed scores of citizens somewhere else. In my brigade, and if not all of the brigades, but in the majority of the brigades various crimes were committed and these services did not deal with these crimes. It states here that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, took a car, took a television set, took a jar of paprika or peppers and -- but did not say that he killed civilians who were innocent. But there is no conviction for any of these things that are mentioned. I don't know who wrote this, who drafted it, but these are just various allegations, information received from someone. But if it exists here, I would like to see an indictment or some kind of sentence or judgement relating to all of these matters that are talked here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So why was it that these things were being written about you and your brigade? Would you like to venture an explanation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: For example, this allegation was written by Sacir Arnautovic. If I'm not mistaken, he's the chief or deputy -- or assistant commander for security for the Ministry of Internal Affairs. But there is another document like this which you showed me yesterday. This is from the Ministry of Internal Affairs. There's a similar document from the Military Security Service. Sefer Halilovic was not on good terms with these services, and even at the beginning of the war there was a quarrel between the minister of MUP, Jusuf Pusina and Sefer Halilovic. Pusina was replaced and Sefer Halilovic remained at his post. So his cooperation with these services was not good, not -- in particular with the military security service where the assistant commander for security at the Supreme Command was a certain person called Muslimovic and the assistant deputy for security was Sacir Arnautovic. So his relationship with them was not good and this was intended to have a negative effect on Sefer Halilovic and not me. That brigade was simply called Sefer's brigade, the 9th Brigade. So I -- this was not something that was supposed to destroy the reputation of the 9th Brigade, but the reputation of Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So according to you, is this truthful or not truthful, what is written in these kind of reports, and I gave you this one as an example?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: There are things that are correct, and that is that the soldiers of the 9th Motorised Brigade did commit criminal acts, they stole a car and did other things. All of this is normal. These things were punished. There are records in the 9th Motorised Brigade. We had a very good, strict security and counter-intelligence service. All of these things were recorded and punished to a certain extent and also passed on for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was Sefer Halilovic aware of these crimes, alleged crimes, of the 9th Motorised Brigade and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Stop there for one moment. A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which crimes we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness has just put the question I was going to put. It should be clarified whether he's being asked about the crimes in that document or the crimes that he's referred to as normal crimes that happened. That should be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, crimes is not such an accurate word.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There may be some disciplinary violations which could not amount to a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was actually referring to what the witness has just previously stated, that the crimes that the 9th Motorised Brigade did in fact commit. I was just talking about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The ones that the witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I'm talking about the crimes that you said that these were normal -- some of the crimes that the 9th Motorised Brigade soldiers committed. And my question was in relation to those crimes only. Was Sefer Halilovic aware of this kind of criminality, the one that you have admitted to, in the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how do you know he knew that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, how could he not have known? I'm sure he did know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you have various -- did you have any discussions in respect of this kind of crimes committed by -- I know you said that other brigades were also -- committed them, but I'm specifically focussing on the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was talk at the Main Staff about some committed -- crimes committed in the 9th Motorised Brigade. This was discussed in the Main Staff. After that, Sefer called me and we talked about the things that were talked about at the main command. So based on that, I conclude that he did know about that those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, did you, as the 9th Brigade, consider yourself within in the military hierarchy? Did you follow orders which were issued to the brigade you were in or were you outside the military hierarchy? How did you perceive yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Look, there isn't a single order that I did not implement. If the Defence is in possession of such a thing, I would like to see it. All orders from the superior command were implemented by the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was your relationship with the 1st Corps command, which was your immediate commander?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I was on good terms with them. We had a good relationship. To the extent that we're talking about combat operations, there were always some misunderstandings there. When an order would come in order to conduct large combat operations when the brigade goes for an attack or several battalions, that is when I would not so much have a conflict with them but I would enter into a discussion in terms of that we shouldn't really be engaging a large number of units because that would always end in a disaster and in the deaths of a large number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what were really the nature of the disagreements that you had with the -- with the command? What kind of things would you disagree, fundamentally disagree, with them about?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It was mostly these things. Not only I myself, but the majority of commanders disagreed with that. Usually at meetings of the corps command there would be a discussion. This would be a meeting with the participation of the corps commander and all the brigade commanders. We would always have these discussions when we were asked to go on the offensive. I wasn't the only one to argue with the 1st Corps commander and deputy commander. Most of the commanders did that. Mostly we wanted to save the lives of our fighters. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So explain to Their Honours why were you against offensive actions and you wanted to confine yourself to defensive actions, which appears to be the fundamental disagreement you had with superior command?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It's evident that we were right. The war is over. I'm talking about Sarajevo only. We were not able to go out or capture anything and they were not able to enter Sarajevo either. The majority of the officers, I don't know if you want me to mention specifically any of their names here, but very shortly before the war broke out in Bosnia the majority of them took part in the planning and setting up of the various lines around Sarajevo. For example, I'm talking about Hadzihasanovic, Enver Hadzihasanovic, who was stationed in the direction of the airport at Mojmilo. He established that line and shelled Sarajevo. So all of these people are now planning these major combat operations to deblock Sarajevo. We didn't have the means to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. If we know that there was a large number of various heavy weapons situated around Sarajevo. We didn't have any of that. We had nothing. We didn't have the means to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. For those same soldiers to ingratiate themselves with the command of the Presidency, they planned these major combat operations, which would imply the deaths of hundreds of people. For them, these were just numbers; but for us, these were our comrades and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this basic philosophy about offensive and defensive actions with Sefer Halilovic? And if you did, what were his views?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about Sarajevo, he was for that. It was -- one of the strongest lines was at Sarajevo. You couldn't do anything in Sarajevo. Outside of Sarajevo, the lines were more elastic, so it was possible to carry out operations of a lesser scale. But as far as Sarajevo was concerned, he was of the opinion that we should not embark on any major operations and that we should stick with defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us about the 10th Brigade. Who was the commander of the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade was Musan Topalovic nicknamed Caco.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was your relationship with him and what was his relationship with the -- with the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: My relationship with him was good, just as it was good with all the other -- just as all the other commanders had a good relationship with him, too. All of them really liked him except for a small number of the former JNA. He couldn't stand former JNA officers, and in his brigade there were no ex-JNA officers at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was the reputation of the 10th Brigade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Look, for a long time nothing was known about the things that he was doing or that he did. Towards the end, sometime in 1993, in mid-1993, it was found out that he was taking civilians away for digging, that some civilians had disappeared, that there was some punishments, but for a long time nobody knew anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier on in your testimony that you did -- there were disciplinary measures taken against soldiers who committed crimes or disciplinary actions. Did you yourself report any of this to the military security for soldiers in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not up to me. I was deputy commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade. It was not for me to report such things, but there were cases of such things being reported. However, in the 9th Motorised Brigade we had a strong military security service. The assistant commander for security was a capable man, Tomislav Juric who was doing his job very well. And all of these things were recorded and punished. There were some cases when if I was the only one who knew about a particular matter and nobody else did, it had to be reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the -- your chief of military security in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Tomislav Juric.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were any prosecutions conducted after the war, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: For crimes or breaches of discipline. Were any prosecutions conducted after the war against soldiers of the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to embark on another subject, so perhaps this might be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a 30-minute break. We'll resume at 11.00, sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you some questions about the practice of trench digging in Sarajevo. Now, was there a practice of trench digging in Sarajevo and how widespread was it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, in some brigades, that was a widespread practice, the digging of trenches. However, in order to prevent that, the Presidency and the supreme command passed a decision for municipalities and their local communes to start collecting people who were fit to work and to send them to the units which had that territory under their area of responsibility in order to dig trenches and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So there was authorised trench digging? This was officially authorised to get men to dig trenches. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there an unauthorised practice, forcing civilians to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In some brigades, yes, that was a practice. In my brigade, that was seldom the case except in certain instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was the -- were the consequences to civilians when they were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: There were many cases where people were killed or wounded, the civilians. However, people worked at the front lines. The lines were just several dozen metres away from the enemy positions and, in certain cases, the consequences were tragic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you elaborate a little bit more. Why was it -- you said because the lines were near the enemy. Why would that make it such a dangerous activity?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the mere fact that the lines were so close to each other, that meant that the people had to work very close to the enemy positions, perhaps some 15 or 20 metres away from the enemy. The enemy could see them very easily and they would start shelling or perhaps they would throw a grenade on the people who were digging. At that time, most of the soldiers were in so-called huts where they were secure from the shelling, while the civilians dug trenches. The people who worked had to dig communication trenches, had to dig trenches for soldiers, and so on. So it was very easy to see them. They were very visible. Although the work was carried out mostly during nighttime, but sometimes it was done also during the day. So these people were an easy target for the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was Sefer Halilovic's position in respect of this trench digging, and I mean the unauthorised trench digging?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Listen, as for this unauthorised, or rather authorised digging is something that the Presidency and the Supreme Command regulated through their decisions. However, there were cases where people would arbitrarily decide to send others to dig trenches, and there were such cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, my question to you was: What was - and that was of course if you know - was Halilovic's position to this unauthorised trench digging?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Look, there would be verbal orders issued, not written ones but verbal, pertaining to certain people who had businesses in Sarajevo or people who were not on good terms with the people from the Supreme Command or the corps. Orders would be issued to take these people to dig trenches. There were also some people who evaded their war duties who were only interested in profiting from the war and other similar activities, and were considered to be hostile. These people would be taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Halilovic ever give an order for anyone to be taken for trench digging service?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In several instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us some examples, please, one by one?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- the case against Halilovic consists of what he knew to be the reputation of the 9th Brigade and this individual as well, this witness as well. There's no case against him of taking people to dig trenches nor has it ever been pleaded, nor was the witness Karavelic asked about any of this. This in my submission, is just character smear, and it is not permitted and I object to the question. It's not relevant to anything that's before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there are any cases that Halilovic gives an order for someone to be taken for the trench digging, it's very obvious evidence to know that Halilovic has the knowledge of these kind of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as you know there's been tendered in evidence a number of documents showing that Halilovic was aware of it and issued orders for it to stop. Now, Your Honours have those in evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. That may be your case. You could elaborate it in your cross-examination of that very point, but however, we'll hear some evidence to the effect that Mr. Halilovic's knowledge rather than his active actions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, as the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, would you please give us these examples and would you just take one at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: There were several examples, but let me give you one pertaining to Mr. Cesko, that's how I knew he was called, who had a private business. I personally was given an order by Sefer Halilovic to take him to dig trenches. He stayed there about seven days digging trenches. On those -- during that time, this man did not eat for seven days while he was digging trenches. After seven days he was taken to a hospital. He left the hospital on his own. Later on, again a decision, or rather on order was issued and the soldiers of the 10th Mountain Brigade arrested him pursuant to that order and he remained with them for about one month.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Any other example which comes to mind?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't know the names of these people; however, there was a gentleman who ran a hotel within my area of responsibility. We took him to dig trenches as well. I don't know other names, but there were such cases where we were issued orders, verbal ones, either by Sefer Halilovic or the commander of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Rasim Delic's son taken to dig trenches to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No. On one occasion he was taken into custody in the 10th Mountain Brigade and beaten up there. Everybody knew about that. Nobody intervened and there were even some orders issued to the effect that this is the fate that should befall him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did -- to your -- did Sefer Halilovic, to your knowledge, know about Rasim Delic's son?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I at that time was in the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade when this son of Rasim Delic was apprehended and another person, either a driver or a security officer of Rasim Delic, Caco, contacted somebody in the command as to inquire whether he should be released. The answer was, no, do not release him. I was even present when this man was beaten, when Rasim Delic's son was beaten and the driver. Later on I asked Caco, who did you talk to. He said he talked to the chief of the Main Staff, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when Sefer asked -- ordered you to take this man Cesko and others, was he aware of the consequences to these people?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, based on previous cases he had to know, because previously there were many instances where people who had been taken to dig trenches were killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic, would you please tell the Court, when did you first meet Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the beginning of the war. I met him then. I did not know him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was your relationship with Halilovic before the war when -- after you met him?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I did not know him before the war. I met him in the beginning of the war, and we were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to take you to 8th June 1993, when there was a shuffle in the army. Can you tell us what that was, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Those were not army shuffles, as you call them. Simply a new position was created. Up until that time there was the chief of the Main Staff position, and later on -- so we did not have the army commander, the supreme commander role was played by Alija Izetbegovic. Later on Rasim Delic came and he was dissatisfied with the fact that he was not appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us why do you say he was dissatisfied. Can you tell us whether you talked to him about it when the news came. Can you please elaborate on that aspect.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: When I learned, or rather I learned from him that a new position was created within the army, that of the army commander, I was called by him to come and see him in his office. I was present when in the building where his office was, Rasim Delic was there with several other members of the General Staff. I saw the gentleman. I saw that he was very angry. He was having an outburst in the office. Several days later, I spoke to him again. We, the commanders, were also somewhat surprised by the creation of this new post and the appointment of Rasim Delic as commander because only about one month later, or rather one month after the war broke out he left the JNA and transferred to the BH Army. He did that only one month after the war broke out, therefore we were surprised as well by his appointment as commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So did you have any discussions in respect of this matter with Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of us were angry. His physical removal was even being mentioned, the removal of Mr. Rasim Delic. Not only in Sarajevo but also outside of Sarajevo, most of the commanders were dissatisfied with Rasim Delic, as were many members of the General Staff. Therefore, his removal was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you mean about his removal. What was discussed in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the physical removal. First we had a plan to issue an ultimatum to the president to remove Rasim Delic from that position and to bring back Sefer Halilovic. If the Presidency failed to go along with that, there were even proposals advanced by some commanders to remove him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, which were -- who were these commanders who were supporting Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly majority of the brigade commanders. The most fervent and vocal supporters were -- was the commander of -- or were the commanders of Delta Unit; the 10th Mountain Brigade; 9th Motorised Brigade; Adnan Solakovic, who was the commander of the Independent Battalion within the corps; and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, who was it that suggested that Delic be removed physically?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: That was mentioned during the conversation, or rather several conversations among ourselves. First of all we wanted to remove him and issue the ultimatum. And following that, his physical removal was discussed. In several instances, Sefer Halilovic himself said that, as did the commander of the Delta unit and finally myself as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was any decision taken as to if that was to be the case who was going to be -- who was going to do it, this removing?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It was said that the Delta unit should take that task upon themselves if things developed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you yourself volunteer?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, in several instances, in various conversations, yes. I applied to carry that out as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what was ultimately decided?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, first something had to be done in order to rehabilitate the reputation of Mr. Sefer Halilovic. That meant that we had to plan a very strong operation which would lead to the rehabilitation and restoring of the credibility and reputation of Sefer Halilovic and would, on the other hand, lead to diminishing the reputation of Rasim Delic. That operation was supposed to be called Obrana Prava 93, which was actually the Neretva 93.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was actually discussed as to what was going to happen in this operation to rehabilitate Sefer Halilovic's reputation and how was the world going to know about it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Since the Neretva valley, or rather Konjic-Jablanica-Mostar, people in that area were very unhappy with the appointment of Rasim Delic for commander. That meant that entire part of Bosnia and Herzegovina supported Sefer Halilovic and we had to plan a well-organised operation, namely to lift the blockade of the town of Mostar. Mostar was in a very difficult situation and the decision, or rather the decision to lift the siege of Mostar would re-establish Sefer Halilovic to the post of commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how was this going to be advertised as well? How were people going to know about these successes?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: There was always an independent journalist around Sefer Halilovic. I think he was a journalist of the Oslobodjenje newspaper and he reported about this operation, the Neretva operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the journalist?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Sefko Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see some of Sefko Hodzic's reports?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did see his reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was your view on his reports?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not proper. For example, at the time it was reported that many features had been taken where -- when in fact that wasn't the case. Then a lot of areas and roads that were supposed to be severed and taken were reported to -- reported as being seized and taken, when in fact it wasn't the case either.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why was that? Why were these reports of military successes of seizing and cutting off roads and seizing territory, why were they reported in that way?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the idea was to show to the people that the introduction of the new command post, and all of the people saw this as a removal of Sefer Halilovic and saw this as a wrong move, and therefore this was done for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, if you knew, what was Sefer Halilovic's position in respect of President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, their relationship was tense, even prior to this removal. And this removal, as it was called, was the culmination of this tense relationship, the relationship between the president and Mr. Sefer Halilovic was really a very tense one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the reaction of the soldiers, just the normal soldiers, to this creation of the new position and Delic being in command, instead of Sefer Halilovic, of the army?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
