utterances.text: Most of the soldiers in Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina supported Sefer Halilovic. And that was visible when they started displaying photographs and posters of Sefer Halilovic in cars, when they started wearing badges with his image, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, previously I showed you MFI 415, that document, where it said that it was you who started this badge wearing. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: A certain butcher came -- a certain person came -- called Mesar came to my unit and he used to accompany Mr. Sefer Halilovic. For example, when Mr. Sefer Halilovic went somewhere, he would be his driver and his security officer. And he brought a number of badges to my unit that we later distributed to other soldiers. So it's not true that I manufactured those badges; I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document, please, and this in respect of badges. It's 65 ter number 168 -- oh, sorry, it's P210. I'd like -- it's a security administration document and I want to draw your attention to the paragraph beginning with: "The source claims that most of the people ..." Have you got that paragraph? It says that: "Most of the people around Ramiz, a.k.a. Celo, are from the Sandjak and they are mostly members of the Military Police Brigade, and all of them are wearing Sefer Halilovic badges." So it was a fact, these badges were being worn? Well, see, this Kenan Kapur and a certain Brus, they were from Prije Polje [phoen]. That was the birth place of Mr. Sefer Halilovic and they knew him personally. The fact that they wore it, they wore it on their own initiative in support of their commander. There was no order that you had to wear something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, were there any consequences for those who did support Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No, not at the time; later, yes. Even regular people expressed their support for Halilovic, not just the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When you say "later" they suffered consequences, can you please tell us what these consequences were.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: All that happened later to some units, brigades, commanders, and so on was a consequence actually of all of this support to Sefer Halilovic, meaning that many people were sentenced or condemned as criminals or as being people who were disobedient because of their support that they showed for Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you give me some examples, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Specifically I'm thinking of Musan Topalovic, Caco. This is the reason why he was killed. I was arrested in 1993 because I gave him support. And it's true, we were misled in a way by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, if Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic give an order, which order would you obey?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Not only I myself, but the majority of commanders in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as fighters at that time would rather carry out an order from Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Halid Cengic.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Cengic. Halid Cengic, if I'm not mistaken was the assistant commander for logistics or something like that or he was the person in charge of logistics. He was a very influential person in the BiH army and in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened to him, but his deputy or some person under him was brutally beaten in some village near Jablanica. I can't remember the man's name. You probably have it somewhere. I think his nickname was Efendija or something like that. So I was called by Mr. Sefer Halilovic to go together with him to that place - I don't know the name of it - where this Efendija person was detained. And on that occasion we were accompanied by Mesar, the commander of the Neretva Brigade, some commander called Homeini - I don't know him - and also Sefer's son. On that occasion I personally saw the questioning of this Efendija, this person under the command of Halid Cengic. They were seeking to find some information out from him, whether he was working for Rasim Delic and Cengic, which he admitted how much money they earned while buying and selling weapons and ammunition. They were asking for information about the negative work of Rasim Delic and Halid Cengic. And on that occasion, this Efendija person was brutally beaten, only because he was Halid Cengic's man.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was it that was doing the beating, just to be quite clear?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: This Mesar person. They took his shoes and socks off and for half an hour they administered a beating on the soles of his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were the others watching that you've just detailed, were these people there watching while this was happening?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Watching and -- yes, they were watching and enjoying the spectacle.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was your and the 9th Brigade's relationship with MUP?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I was on pretty good terms with the MUP. However, in view of my relationship with Mr. Sefer Halilovic, they were always trying to disrespect me, to be disrespectful towards me as a deputy commander of the 9th Brigade and as a fighter. Any fighter who committed anything wrong in the 9th Brigade, their acts were ascribed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did something happen on 9th June with yourself and MUP?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: This was not specifically related to the MUP. I don't recall the exact date, but the military security administration whose chief or commander was Muslimovic ordered the arrest of the deputy commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, Senad Pecar, which resulted in unrests later in some parts of the brigades. At that same time, a major assault was being conducted at the -- against the 2nd Viteska Brigade. And during the fiercest period of the attack, they decided to arrest Senad Pecar covertly, knowing what the consequences of all of that would be, knowing what the reaction would be of the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade. Still, they did arrest him and this later led to unrest and rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you informed that you might be arrested?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: After the arrest of Senad Pecar, the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade went crazy. We both called Mr. Sefer Halilovic. We said what was going on, why was he arrested? He said he doesn't know. This was something that was done by Muslimovic, who Sefer Halilovic hated above all. And he said that it could be very likely that we would also be arrested. I didn't see any reason why I would be arrested, but there you go. That was the information I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And did Sefer Halilovic call you on this matter again and how many times, if so?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In terms of this rebellion we did speak on several occasions with Mr. Sefer Halilovic and he -- we said more or less that we wanted Muslimovic's replacement. He was the chief of the security administration. We demanded this later. And he was replaced later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was it that Sefer Halilovic was telling you in these conversations over this rebellion? What were you supposed to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as the rebellion is concerned, I really don't know. I know that I was in contact with him and that was that. He asked for the replacement of Mr. Muslimovic, which meant that we were actually demanding his replacement. I don't remember whether he requested anything else. We had a meeting after that with the president and others, and we did tell them that we wanted to have Muslimovic replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was he replaced?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I think that he was replaced later. I know that he was replaced later, that a new deputy commander for security was appointed, and that was Jusuf Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic, I want to take you to another subject matter and I want to ask you, were you present at a meeting in Zenica when Operation Neretva was discussed with some commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would object to that one. Your Honours, it's got two questions in it and a proposition the witness hasn't quite gotten round to agreeing to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's establish that meeting first and then later on we'll come to the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was trying to be economical with the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, was there a meeting with Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there a meeting with the 1st Corps commander, Karavelic, to discuss Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: At the time when this action was being planned, I was called to see Sefer Halilovic. The commander of the 1st Corps, Vahid Karavelic, was invited to attend, too. They probably talked before that and I concluded that during a later conversation. Sefer Halilovic requested that units of the 9th Motorised Brigade or part of the 9th Motorised Brigade units, the Delta unit, the Adnan Solakovic's Independent Battalion and some units of the 10th Mountain Brigade, around 300 fighters all together, should be completely armed in order to be able to conduct combat operations in the sector of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic was against issuing such an order because he considered that the lines of defence of Sarajevo would be weakened by such actions and therefore he was categorically against such an order. That is why Sefer Halilovic called us in to attend this meeting. He called the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, the commander of Delta, Adnan Solakovic, and myself, so that we could tell them that we were able to set aside units which could take part in this action, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So could you tell -- why did Halilovic ask for these specific troops that you have just stated?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: He asked -- well, for example, as far as units of the 9th Motorised Brigade are concerned, that brigade was able to allocate a certain number of fighters completely equipped, which Mr. Sefer Halilovic requested. The other units also were able to do that without weakening the lines in their area of responsibility. They were able to leave. On the other hand, all that we had planned -- according to all that we had planned, these units were supposed to get out and leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was Sefer Halilovic's relationship with Vahid Karavelic, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: From what I could see, it was a formal, official, relationship. For example, Mr. Karavelic was very categorical in regards of having soldiers leave Sarajevo at the request of Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and this is how I could tell. But I also did know that their relationship was strained. They spoke very formally to each other. There was no friendliness or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And at this meeting, what was the general mood, if you can describe it, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. This question seems to me a bit -- well, you know about the general mood. But as it seemed to me, Vahid Karavelic was not in favour of soldiers of the 1st Corps leaving Sarajevo in any event. And this was something that was obvious later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you some orders and I will start with P161. You will see it in a minute on the ELMO -- on the -- this is an order from Sefer Halilovic to the commander of the 1st Corps, Vahid Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, all these four orders I'm going to show you, are they in accord with what was decided at this meeting about the deployment of the troops?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. I didn't hear it very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: These are all deployment orders -- I've just showed you the first one and we are limited in e-court, we can only show you one at a time. Are they in accord with what had been agreed in the meeting with Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it has to be done order by order, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Take this first one, what is that order saying? What is the purport of that order, just very quickly? If you look at the order on your screen.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Before this order, there were meetings where Mr. Karavelic was expressly against any kind of -- of units leaving Sarajevo in any way. Then we have order number 2, which states that if you believe that the defence -- that such redeployment endangers Sarajevo, I am prepared to bear full responsibility. So Karavelic was against having units leave Sarajevo, but Sefer Halilovic then convinced Karavelic and issued -- and then also on the basis of orders, Karavelic did later agree that -- to send out these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now, if you would now please look at P382, it will come up on your screen in a minute. This is an order from Halilovic to Karavelic. What is the purport of this order?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: We were supposed to leave originally on the 3rd of September, 1993; however, Karavelic did not fulfil that order. We were not prepared, we were not ready. So then this order came to the 1st Corps and sought the urgent departure of the units, but we actually did not leave because Karavelic was not in favour of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now if I can show you, please, an order dated 4th September from Karavelic to yourself. Would you look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: P383, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the 9th Motorised Brigade received this order, it's familiar -- is informed about this order, and it implemented this order. There was just a slight problem regarding this order. The oral agreement we had during the meeting with Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the order was made that the unit of the 9th Motorised Brigade should provide around 100 or 150 soldiers; however, the commander of the 1st Corps actually requested two platoons numbering approximately 25 fighters each. The command of the 9th Motorised Brigade began to effect or execute this order and it instructed the battalion commanders and some units to allocate this number of soldiers, about 100 to 150, which the Motorised Brigade command did. They assembled in front of the 9th Motorised Brigade command; however, Mr. Karavelic came and he attended the line-up or the review of this unit and issued an oral order that the unit should be halved and that 50 men should be sent to the Jablanica sector. On that occasion, Vahid Karavelic personally lined up the unit again and halved it and sent them off to the Jablanica sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now I'll show you another order which is P290, an order dated 5th September, 1993, from Karavelic to Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Can you tell us about this order, please. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn up the volume a bit. No, I'm sorry, could you please zoom in on the document, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It will be done in a minute. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please tell us what this order is about, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The relocation of the units from Sarajevo was not conditional on the time; it was actually up to Mr. Karavelic. So it's not true that there was a major storm. We were not able to leave because the superior command of the corps and the Supreme Staff could not agree amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So was it delayed, the leaving of your troops?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, as -- we know that Sefer Halilovic was the Chief of Staff. Now, was he authorised to issue such orders to launch an operation like Operation Neretva in your view?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did have such orders, such authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell us what in your view was the structure of subordination of the troops for Operation Neretva? What were you informed about how the subordination was going to work in military terms for this operation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In some conversations with Mr. Sefer Halilovic but first of all with the immediate superior, the commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade, Vahid Karavelic, the conclusion was reached that these units should remain for seven days in the Jablanica sector in order to carry out combat operations. And these units from Sarajevo were to provide men for a battalion and then the battalion would have its own commander. I think it was supposed to be Senad Pecar if I'm not mistaken. And they would be immediately resubordinated to the Zulfikar unit, that was the Zulfikar unit, the actually the commander of the unit, Zulfikar Alispago, or actually the commander of the Sarajevo 2 operations group. The units would be resubordinated to them. The commander hierarchy was the battalion commander of the Sarajevo unit, Senad Pecar, then Zulfikar Alispago, and then Zulfikar Alispago was the commander of that axis, and the commander, the final commander at the end of the chain of command was Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what date was this subordination to start when it came to your troops, the 9th Brigade, what was the date that they were subordinated to Zulfikar Alispago?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Look, the mere appointment of the battalion commander meant that from that moment on the commander was to carry out all orders of Zulfikar Alispago. So from the departure onwards, from the time that unit arrived in Jablanica, that unit was under the command of Alispago or Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how was the command of the axis of attacks configured?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the entire operation stretched from Prozor, or rather from Bugojno to Mostar, so there were several axes. The command of the entire operation was Mr. Sefer Halilovic. There were several directions of attack, and I don't know who the commanders were there. But in the area where the Sarajevo commanders were was under the command of Zulfikar Alispago. Among others, there were also assistants, or rather members of the General Staff, Rifat Bilajac, Zicro, Vehbija Karic, and so on. There were several there who were members of the General Staff, and their role there was to assist the axis commanders, in terms of the operative portion, the planning, and the execution of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I request the usher to bring me the Operation Neretva map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I should have said it earlier, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic, would you look at that map, please. Have you seen that map before?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when was that? When was the first time you saw it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw this map was sometime on the second or third day after the crime in Grabovica. I did not see it beforehand, but I knew roughly what areas were to be attacked and so on. So I saw it two or three days upon my arrival in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And could you explain to Their Honours, please, the axis of attack for Zulfikar Alispago where your -- members of your unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a leading question there. This witness has admitted to having any involvement with these troops when they're involved in these combat activities at all. And it had better be clarified what the -- is meant by "your unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The witness testified that he saw this map on the second or third day after the crime in Grabovica, but he knows roughly what areas to attack on. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that's what I understood, Your Honour, and the question seemed to contain a proposition that the witness hasn't agreed to. So it's up to him to agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you may clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Just to clarify my question, was units of the 9th Brigade which has been subordinated to Alispago, which axis of attack were they supposed to be on, if you could point it out, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is in very small script, so I can't see it well. But this is roughly in this area towards the area of Vrda. I know the elevations that were to be attacked, Medved and so on. I know the exact spot where action was supposed to be carried out, but this was the axis under the command of Zulfikar Alispago, under those command the units from Sarajevo were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see the other axis? How many axes are there in total?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: There was several axes. I don't know how many commanders there were on these axes, but I know there were several. In order to lift the siege of Mostar, one needed to have several axes. What I know is that there was several of them and then I know about the axes under the command of Zulfikar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you're familiar with that terrain, are you, yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not exactly familiar with it, but I know some things about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- there are two signatures on that map. Can you look at the map and see -- there's a signature on the top left-hand corner and a signature on the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know both signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Whose are they, to begin with?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The upper one is the signature of the army commander, Rasim Delic; and the lower one is the signature of the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Does that hold any significance for you as a military person?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, that means that the commander of the entire operation, or rather the approval of this operation was done by Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic. Based on what I see here, this is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Delalic. Now, I'd like to take you to the time when your troops -- the actual selection of the troops. Can you describe to us how was it that they were selected, the ones which did go down, and where was this done?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The selection of the soldiers was conducted in the 9th Motorised Brigade. When such selection is carried out, selection of such a large number of people, commanders of battalions are always invited to select several soldiers and to send them to the brigade command. So the composition of these soldiers was such that they were not all from one unit. They were from different units, or rather, different battalions and staff units. The selection of the personnel was carried out by battalion commanders together with the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you have any decision-making in this process as to which men actually were to go down to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade issues an order. The commander or the deputy commander cannot make selection by going from one soldier to the next and selecting them. No, they issue an order to the battalion commanders or to the commander of the reconnaissance company or an assault company. And out of all those units, a selection is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to belabour this, but can you tell us, like, physically outside what happened, were the soldiers lined up? Or were they picked? I mean, how exactly did it happen? More specifically, which soldiers were chosen?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Look here, the commander of the corps, when issuing an order to the brigade commander to allocate a company or so many soldiers, this is not something that is done personally by a commander who selects them personally. In the same way, the brigade doesn't do it either. They don't go from soldier to soldier selecting them personally. So the order that we saw here is analogous to the order issued by the 9th Motorised Brigade to commanders to establish a company numbering so many soldiers. For example, commander of the 1st Battalion sent four people; commander to the 2nd Battalion, ten people; commander of the 3rd Battalion sent four people, and so on and so on. So the composition of this unit that was sent to Jablanica was a mixed one, and that was pursuant to the order coming from the corps. They needed infantry soldiers, they needed people experienced in anti-armoured weaponry, they needed reconnaissance people, and so on. So this unit had to be of a mixed make-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So how many men were ready to -- to set out to Herzegovina at the end of this process?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Since the first order that we saw here stated that the 9th Motorised Brigade had to send about 100 to 120 soldiers, this is exactly the number that the brigade gathered and lined up in front of the command. However, when Vahid Karavelic came, he did not agree with this and he followed the text of the soldiers, indicating that 50 soldiers were needed. The people were lined up in two lines. Vahid Karavelic tried to select soldiers personally. He first gave a speech to them in strong moral terms about them needing to go to Jablanica to conduct a combat operation. He told them about the situation in Mostar. He told them what they could expect down there, that they could be killed or wounded, and so on. It's a typical speech held by a commander under such circumstances. And then he proceeded to split the unit in half. First he asked for volunteers. He said that 120 was not needed. He asked for volunteers and he said that he needed about roughly 50 people. However, when he asked for volunteers, everybody applied, everybody came forward. And then since the unit was lined up in two rows, he ordered them to stand at attention. They stood at attention. Then he said, "First row come forward." The first row came forward. Then he said, "The first row will go and the second row is dismissed." This is how that unit was made up, the unit that was sent to the Jablanica sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And of all the people -- of all the men from your particular brigade, out of them how many were of them were from the 9th, these particular men -- sorry, I'll re-ask -- I'll ask -- I'll ask another question. What was your assignment in relation to this operation, your assignment personally, if you had one?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: My assignment was nothing special. It was nothing that differed from the task of the 9th Motorised Brigade. The task was for the 9th Motorised Brigade. That brigade had to send a unit in order to carry out combat operations in the Jablanica sector. My task specifically was to send not 50 but 120 soldiers because that was the oral order issued to me by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, that was the arrangement. So that was the agreement reached at the first and second meeting, namely to send 120 soldiers there. The interpreters keep insisting that I speak slower; that's why I'm making pauses.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's all right. What I want to know, Mr. Delalic, is: Did you have a role to play in Operation Neretva yourself? Were you supposed to accompany your troops to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you have any role in Operation Neretva personally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No. There are orders and there is the naming of the command personnel. And finally I was the deputy commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade. I wasn't the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, were you signaling for a break at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if it's proper for you --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm entirely in your hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we hear the witness and I saw Mr. Weiner is here in the courtroom, I have a question to put to you concerning with the expert report. I believe on the last Friday we have received the Defence motion concerning use and tendering of the military expert report. I just want to know whether the Prosecution would like to reply to this report or not, and if so when? Because we have to act as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Court told us that our response was due today, and that's what they're doing right now, they're responding to the motion. We received it late Friday, but we are responding to it and we met yesterday and also we were in on Sunday, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And another matter is that I believe that I reminded you that if you want to furnish any reports, so-called amended reports, it has to be agreed upon by the expert himself, at least he himself should sign that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that's the basis we could receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, your legal officer contacted us on Friday to also remind us of that, to get a signature from the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I hope we could make a decision this week concerning of the expert report. I don't think the Defence would like to file a reply on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No, I just wondered if -- I think Your Honour asked a question, but has the witness signed that report as yet or not, is a query we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I just reminded them that if they want to furnish us a report and that report should be agreed upon by the expert witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour's right about that. I just had an inquiry, though, has it been signed yet? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, are you in the position to respond to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I know we were in this weekend; the expert wasn't. So we are trying to get ahold of him today. We are trying to contact him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least not up to now, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic, we were talking about your troops going to Herzegovina. When did they leave to go to Herzegovina, the troops which were designated to go down there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the line-up of the troops was over, Mr. Vahid Karavelic, the corps commander, ordered the unit to move and to go to a place where the tunnel under the runway was. They had to wait for the dark in order for the unit to pass through the tunnel during the nighttime because there was always shelling there and they were afraid that some soldiers could be killed. So they had to wait for the dark to fall to go through the tunnel. And upon exiting the tunnel, the shelling was constant. And they, for a while, put these soldiers in some premises in order to protect them. However, the trucks that were needed to transport the soldiers weren't ready either, and the soldiers were to be transported in several phases. The trucks were provided for them to take them up to the Igman Mount. The trucks, however, weren't ready. And the problems arose at that point. For a while, the soldiers had to deal with bad weather and they remained there for several hours. I was called to come to Hrasnica, to help with providing the trucks. The trucks or the buses were supposed to be provided by the brigade commander in Hrasnica, Fikret Plevljak, and when I was told that the problems arose, I and my escorts went to Hrasnica. We also had to pass through the tunnel. And I tried to arrange the transportation. The order for me to go there was issued by Vahid Karavelic; it was a verbal order. I was supposed to help them. A lot of soldiers were dissatisfied with their situation and wanted to go back to Sarajevo. Therefore, I was issued an order to go there and to provide assistance and prevent the soldiers from going back to Sarajevo. So my arrival in Hrasnica was meant to ensure that the trucks would be provided as soon as possible, and the troops departed towards Bradina and towards the Igman Mount. When I arrived in Hrasnica, or rather at Igman, which was quite difficult, there were new trucks awaiting the soldiers there. The easiest part of the road is the one leading to Bradina. I went with them in order to prevent new problems from arising en route. The first place where we stopped to rest was Bradina. Bradina is a place right below Konjic, perhaps 10 kilometres below Konjic. The soldiers had a rest there, and then they continued their trip towards Jablanica, or rather towards the base and command of Zulfikar Alispago. We split at that point. I went back to Konjic and the troops, with their commander Senad Pecina continued towards Bradina. What kind of accommodation they were given there and what happened there is something that I don't know. In Konjic I went to see my friend Almir Habibija and his wife Alma. Almir Habibija incidentally was in charge of procuring materiel and technical equipment for the 9th Motorised Brigade, rather for collecting and purchasing various weapons, and occasionally I would go to him to fetch that equipment and take it back to Sarajevo. Therefore, I went to Konjic to see him and to see how much equipment had been collected in the meantime. I spent the night there. On the following day at around 10.00 --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, I'm sorry to interrupt you but I want to take you slowly through this evidence. Okay. Now, you arrived in Konjic, but before you got there and perhaps it will also assist you on the date, I would like to show you this document and this is P207. It's a document from the state security services. Have you got it in your screen now?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is about an incident which happened on 8 September at 0430 hours in the morning. Can you tell us about this? What is this? What are they reporting on?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as I know and as far as I could see, there were several members - I'm not sure whether they were members of the police or members of the army - but at any rate they were there at the checkpoint near Hadzici. I'm not sure what that place is called. They refused to remove from the checkpoint or from this street the obstacles. There was something there that was intended as an obstacle. They did not want to remove it until we produced some documents. These members were a bit -- not a bit, but quite drunk, and the soldiers were irritated by that how -- because the soldiers are the ones who go into combat and can be killed, and then all of a sudden there are these three or four soldiers making trouble for them. That was our checkpoint. I don't know who secured it, whether it was the police or the army. So it turned out that they had a scuffle there. I don't know whether somebody hit somebody else. I'm not sure what happened, but after a brief altercation, they continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So the important thing to note here is the date, which is 8 September at 0430 hours, for that is the time, would you agree, that you were at this particular checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was in the morning hours, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's right. And then you said you went to Konjic and you went to your friend's house, Habibija's. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I go into private session, please, for a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic, the next morning what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: My task and job was not to go to the Jablanica sector at all. However, since I had been in the Konjic and Jablanica sector on several occasions before in order to obtain equipment and materiel, a few -- on an occasion -- on a previous occasion when I was out there, I bought an anti-aircraft cannon, a DSK, for which I had paid 18.000 German marks, so I went to purchase that anti-aircraft gun. At the moment there are court proceedings going on in Sarajevo in relation to that matter. I am tried for exceeding my official duties at the time. This is still ongoing. So at that time, I was going to get this weapon, together with the things I would pick up from Almir Habibija, and I was supposed to return to Sarajevo with those things. However, when I came to Zulfikar Alispago's base, I found out about -- I think this was sometime in the afternoon, I found out about the crime which had taken place in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Zuka's base, as you said it was in the afternoon, that would be on the 8th, right, the same day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this leading has got to stop. The witness can say when he arrived and not be told when he arrived by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's come to that step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought the witness had said he went the same day and I apologise if he hadn't. And I will indeed go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When did you go to Zuka's base?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I said that earlier. I took my leave of Almir Habibija. I left his apartment around 10.00 or 11.00. It's been a while since then, about 12 or 13 years, so I can't really remember everything exactly. But in any case, sometime in the morning at 10.00 or 11.00, I left Habibija's apartment and set off for Zuka's base. When I arrived at Zuka's base, it was the afternoon. And as I said, in front of Zuka's base I met Nihad Bojadzic, Zuka's deputy, the deputy commander of the Zulfikar unit, and Mr. Zulfikar, too, who told me right away that some people not from my unit, from the 9th Motorised Brigade, but from the units which had arrived from Sarajevo committed certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this was told to you by Zulfikar, you said?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who else was there? Can you please tell us the names of all those who were present at Zuka's base when you arrived there, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I parked my car in front of Zuka's base, in front of Zulfikar Alispago's command. The first person who told me of that was Nihad Bojadzic, Zuka's deputy and Zuka himself. Zuka, Nihad, and I went into the office immediately where Mr. Sefer Halilovic was sitting and some members of the Main Staff. This was actually Zuka's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you remember the names of these people from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: When I say "several of them, I am -- I mean two or three people. I think Vehbija Karic was there, Suljo -- I can't remember the names at the moment. Zicro -- I can't remember the names at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Delalic, I want to take this slowly. What did Sefer Halilovic say to you, if he said anything at all?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Zulfikar Alispago and Nihad Bojadzic first told me about the crime. I went inside. Not much attention was being paid to the actual crime, I think, from what I called see at least. Very briefly I saw that they were discussing this crime, this alleged crime that had taken place. The only thing that was known was that some people were -- had killed some civilians there in the course of the night, but no conversation -- the conversation did not actually touch upon what had to be done. It was more about some grenades, mountain cannon, and Howitzers that had to be obtained. That was more the thrust of the conversation when I came in. After spending a brief period of time there, Mr. Sefer Halilovic told Zuka to go to Grabovica and to see what was happening down there. When Zuka left, I also asked for permission to go there because I was interested to know what had happened because there was also mention of members of the 9th Motorised Brigade. So in Zuka's Jeep, Zuka and I set off towards Grabovica. At the very entrance to Grabovica as soon as you cross --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, I still want to go back to that, Zuka's base, if I may. Was there anything in the conversation which suggested to you for how long they had known about these alleged crimes in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: It's possible that they had already found out about it during the night or early in the morning, because some refugees had managed to flee from the scene of the crime and they were perhaps stopped by some fighters of Zulfikar Alispago at the exit to Grabovica. So it's possible that the crime was already known about by morning or in the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you said Zuka was asked to go down, and you requested to go down. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you asked to do anything when you got down there? Were you issued with any instructions or orders?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Nobody issued any orders except to say that we should look and then report back about what had happened and was happening down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there any indication that the killings had stopped?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you ordered to take any action with respect of -- in fact, arrests of any soldiers, isolate them, or do anything when you got there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever say to Sefer Halilovic, I don't think you should go down there because it might be dangerous?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't know any reason why I would tell him something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you think the situation might be dangerous for you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense you mean. Why would it be dangerous?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The fact that there had been murders going on in a given area, would you consider that to be a dangerous situation for yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I didn't consider the situation to be dangerous. I still didn't know exactly what it was all about, other than what I was told, that there was a crime that had occurred there and that members of units that had come from Sarajevo had committed certain killings. I didn't see any danger there for me or any danger for Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what time did you set off with Zuka to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon sometime. I really can't tell exactly what time it was. Perhaps I can just speculate. Maybe it was about 2.30 or 3.30, something like that. I really don't know exactly, but judging by subsequent events it was probably sometime between 2.30, 3.30, or 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. So did you get to the village?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It wasn't too far away, maybe some 15 minutes from Zuka's base. We arrived and as soon as we crossed a small bridge from the left to the right bank of the Neretva River, right after the bridge some 10 metres away we saw a trail along the street, along the asphalt as if something had been dragged along there, something bloody had been dragged along there. Zuka got out of the car and started to follow that trail. He called me to do the same thing, so we were just following that trail below the road towards the lake. There were one or two bodies very close to the water. We sat in the car right away, and about some 100 or 150 metres away from that spot is a village where the soldiers were billeted. On the road there, we met a guard who was guarding that exit at a ramp. We asked the guard -- Zuka asked him if he knew anything about those bodies that we saw, and he said that he didn't know anything about that. He allowed us through and we were walking around amongst the soldiers, asking them if they had heard anything. We couldn't find out anything more than that, other than the fact that some shooting was heard during the night, but none of the soldiers wanted to say anything about it. I don't know whether they were trying to protect each other or something, but we didn't really find out anything much. We didn't spend too long there. We returned and Zuka informed Mr. Sefer that the information was correct, that some Croatian civilians were killed in the village of Grabovica. And after that, nothing was done in order to prevent possible new crimes or to punish them. I stayed there for 10 or 15 minutes and I was informed by a radio that two boys had been found in the woods above the village of Grabovica, so I hurried there. The logistics person who was in charge of the battalion of the Sarajevo units at that point actually came to pick up the food for the soldiers, and I went back to the village of Grabovica together with him and I saw those two children. When they told me everything that they knew --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, I have to slow you down a little, please. I want to take you back to Zuka's base, when you returned there and you reported what you had seen. Could you please tell Their Honours what did Sefer Halilovic say to you and your report, your findings?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Zulfikar Alispago submitted the report. He said what it was that we saw and said that there were indications that some killings were committed there. Mr. Sefer Halilovic did not react in the way he should have reacted, meaning that measures which should have been taken were not taken. At no point did I hear an order being issued to locate the perpetrators of those crimes or to inform the commander of the unit to find those persons and to arrest them and so on. All in all, he did not react the way he should have reacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you were given no instructions at that time what to do?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No. The offensive was still the topic of the conversation, the offensive. Neither he nor any of his colleagues from the General Staff took any steps to find out who the perpetrators were or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But what was being said about the offensive, Operation Neretva, in relation to this incident? What were they discussing about it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: When Zulfikar Alispago and I entered the office, Zuka interrupted a conversation that was underway for preparations of the offensive, deployment of long-range weapons, and so on. Because -- also about obtaining some shells from Zenica, all the shells or the grenades came from Zenica. And then Zuka said that he had seen and that also I had seen some bodies thrown near the river. After that, the conversation was halted for a little bit and then it continued again on the subject of planning of the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you were down in the village, did the soldiers say anything to you about their accommodation at the time you were at the village?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: See, we spent a very short amount of time in the village, perhaps 15 minutes or so. I don't know exactly how long, but we were there for a very short time. Most of the soldiers did not have accommodation. We actually found them lying around in the fields, in the grass, and so on because allegedly the hosts of the Croat houses where they were supposed to be billeted wouldn't let them in; that was the story. So a large number of the fighters were actually billeted in front of the houses of some of those people. Some of the soldiers did manage to get accommodation inside the houses, but most of them were sleeping outside and were not able to get the accommodation. Specifically Zuka went from house to house asking about accommodation, but all in all we found out that there was shooting in the course of the night, that there were killings, but nobody wanted to talk about it, nobody had seen anything. Zuka reported to Mr. Halilovic about everything that he had seen. Q Were you ever told about a meeting which was held in Grabovica with the General Staff by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: After the crime I learned that a large number of the fighters objected to the type of billeting in Grabovica, they didn't have any place to stay -- there was no place for them to stay. The owners, the Croat owners of the houses did not want to let them in. Somebody from the General Staff did come by, but what I want found out was that Vehbija Karic was there amongst other things who actually told me why the soldiers were sleeping in front of the houses and that Mr. Karic was quite categorical in saying that if need be they should use force in order to enter the houses and that if there were any Croats who were creating problems in terms of providing the accommodation, should be just thrown into the lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did your soldiers say to you that they took these remarks of Vehbija Karic seriously?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I didn't really ask them about it during those few days. It wasn't logical. But it's very likely that some of the soldiers took that seriously; that was to be expected. It was an expected reaction. Those who planned that had to take into account that these people who were going to attack Croats were supposed to be billeted in Croat homes. Certain -- a certain number of incidents should have been expected in such circumstances and perhaps even that some crimes would take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did your soldiers ever tell you who was present at the time Vehbija Karic made those remarks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Vehbija Karic was there as well as someone else from the General Staff, but I never found out who that was. I recall just what Vehbija Karic said, and that's something that has stuck with me as something characteristic. It didn't make sense to me that any of those people could actually say something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did your soldiers inform you whether Sefer Halilovic was present when Vehbija Karic made those remarks?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: You see, later, the information I had later…I mean, a lot of soldiers said that he had not been there. Some said he had, some said that Zuka had been there as well, and a few other members of the General Staff. I cannot tell you with certainty who was there and who wasn’t. However, like I told you, many soldiers said that he had been there and then again many said that he hadn’t. But what I can recall, and what soldiers probably…what was said by Vehbija Karic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, were you aware where your soldiers were going to be billeted when they were released to go into Herzegovina? Had anybody discussed this matter of billeting with you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I think that this was discussed in Jablanica -- actually, I think there was talk that they would be billeted in Jablanica. There was never any mention of Grabovica or any Croat villages in that sense. I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you ever shown Diva Grabovica by anyone as a possible to accommodate troops?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember anyone mentioning it or not, but I don't think that this was mentioned, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you go and look at Diva Grabovica yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Before the soldiers were billeted there?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: No, never because Diva Grabovica had just been liberated. That village under the control of the Croatian army, so I never actually went there before then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you see it from a distance?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some two or three months before that because an action was discussed that my unit could participate in and I went and looked at that place through binoculars from a distance of some 4 or 5 kilometres I observed the village. But you couldn't really say that we saw houses themselves, but we could see some positions of Croat soldiers and I knew more or less what was being discussed. However, I never wanted to take part in that and later Zuka's unit and some other units, I don't know which ones, captured that village and placed it under B and H army control.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you with anyone at the time you saw this Diva Grabovica through binoculars?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before that question is answered, I just want it to be made very clear whether this witness distinguishes between the village of Grabovica and the location Diva Grabovica or whether he thinks they're the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is Diva Grabovica and Grabovica the same place according to you? Are they two different locations or one?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know if these are two different locations. There is a left side and a right side, though. What's what, I'm not sure. I know exactly where positions of the Croatian army were, and all of that was under Croatian control. But I don't know whether Diva Grabovica and Grabovica are one in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you saw what we for now will describe as Diva Grabovica through binoculars, were you looking at the village of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: You couldn't really see the village itself. I've already said that. You could only see some points held by the Croatian army and the lines of the Croatian army. It was very hard to see the village itself. Perhaps just the odd house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you're not quite clear whether these are one in the same thing -- place?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's go to when you -- you went back to the village, you said, because you heard that two boys had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before that question is asked, Your Honour, this has been left in a very unsatisfactory state. There's a map. The question can be dealt with very quickly, and it just leads to unnecessary confusion in this case because the Prosecution have put a cast on Diva Grabovica in their opening statement. I don't want there to be any vagueness about this, and in my submission at the moment, I don't want to paraphrase what the witness says or what he means. But it just has to be made clear whether or not when he talks about the village he saw through binoculars he's talking about Diva Grabovica or is he talking about Grabovica, the village where these events subsequently happened. It's a fairly simple question, but it really needs to be clarified, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the purpose of cross-examination was exactly that. The witness has been quite clear. I asked him three times and he's said it very clearly he doesn't know; it was very far away. Perhaps counsel can clarify that for himself during cross-examination. I don't think there's anymore purpose in me continuing with this unless Your Honours would like me to ask him again, which of course I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if the witness testifies he does not know which one is which, I believe we have to stop here. Maybe in the cross-examination the Defence could explore on that point. Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I was talking about that -- you saw -- you heard about two boys. Can you please tell us about that. You went back to the village and what did you find?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: In front of one of the houses where the soldiers were billeted I saw several soldiers of the 9th Motorised Brigade. There were soldiers from other units there as well although I did not know them. Together with the two boys whom I later learned were named Zadro Goran and Zadro Zoran, or Vedran or something like that. So immediately upon my arrival I asked them about their names and about their families. The boys were scared. They were cold, they were hungry, they were miserable. Before I started talking to them, I asked the soldiers whether anybody had any food to give the boys. Then I started talking to the boys and they told me a terrible, an absolutely terrible story about how their parents were killed, grandmother and grandfather as well, and their 3-year-old sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, before we carry on with that I would like to show you a picture. Perhaps you will -- then we will of course hear about this. And it's P3, please. You will be asked to mark on this photograph, and you will be assisted. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, first, can you mark for us where your soldiers told you that they found the children and put a circle around that place.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who found the children said that they had found them above the railway, which was here. You can see it here in the picture above the village. It would be roughly here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. So if you can just mark the photograph, please, with a circle and put "found children."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's a good clue. Have we succeeded?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, if you could just mark that place with a circle or a cross, whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And if you can write in that circle, please, "found children."

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you also now mark for us on that photograph where it is that you found the children, when you talked to them, when you went there.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you write in there, please, "talked to children" -- "talked." The word "talked" would be good enough.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that photograph into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P416.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, could you please, Mr. Delalic, briefly tell us what the children said to you when you talked to them.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: One of the boys told me that during the previous night some soldiers had come and asked his father and the grandfather to show them the stable. They did that. They went out to the stable. And after a certain period of time they heard shots. The boys had remained with the mother in the room where they were. So after a certain period of time they heard shots, and the mother threw the two of them out through the window and told them to run to the friend's house or perhaps to their uncle's house who lived near the railway in the area that I marked here. I'm not sure. So the boys jumped out through the window and went to these friends or their uncle and aunt's house, as their mother had told them, and found them killed there, found that these people were killed there. The boys hid in the forest, waited until the morning there. They were hungry but stayed there in the forest. They were cold. They were hungry. And as a result of that, they went out to the railway where some soldiers came across them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was your reaction to what they had said to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC
utterances.text: The first thing I asked them was whether they knew about what had happened with their parents and children, and they said that all of them had been killed and started crying. I asked them whether -- since I was quite appalled by this story, I asked them whether they could recognise any of the soldiers. And one boy addressed me as "uncle" and said, "Uncle," as long as I live, I will not forget that face. At that point I got up, took my pistol out, took the boy who told me the story by the hand. The other boy kept quiet because he was very scared. He kept crying constantly and did not utter a word. So the boy that told me the story who was more open, I took him by the hand and, as I was angry, I asked him whether he could recognise any of the soldiers sitting around us. As he was unable to recognise any of them, all of the soldiers who were there in the vicinity, I told them to approach us. There were some soldiers that I didn't know there. There was soldiers from the 10th Mountain Brigade, from the 9th Motorised Brigade, and so on. So all of those soldiers, I told them to stand in line, and I was threatening them with my pistol. And I took the boy or the boys by the hand and then we went from one soldier to the next to see if he could recognise them. As I've said, not all of the soldiers were present there. Some had gone out to reconnaissance assignments, some had gone to Jablanica, and the boys were unable to recognise the perpetrators among the soldiers lined up there. I was prepared to kill somebody right there at the spot, as I was quite revolted by the story. Therefore, I was prepared for something so radical. But at any rate, I got the children -- I put the children into the car and I drove them to Zuka's base. Upon arriving at the base, I took them to the area where Zuka's office was, where the forward command post was, and where Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Zulfikar Alispago normally assembled. In front of that office, there was a conference area and a dining area, and I put the children at the table. They sat down. Zulfikar Alispago and Nihad Bojadzic were there at the entrance, and I told them about the children and briefly described how their parents, grandparents, and 3-year-old sister had been killed, to which Zuka replied that I shouldn't have brought them there but should have killed them en route. I cursed at him quite angrily and I told him if he had a heart to do that, he should do it himself. After that, I entered the office where Mr. Sefer Halilovic was and several members of the Main Staff. Zulfikar followed me into that office, and I told the people assembled there briefly that I had brought with me two children whose family had been killed and that they should see for themselves what to do with the children and that they should hear out their story. After telling the story of the two children, the first reaction of Mr. Sefer Halilovic and everybody else assembled there was that they didn't want to hear anything about any children, that the children should be removed, that dirty laundry ought to be removed, and that the offensive ought not to be endangered and so on. I asked them to let me bring the children in so that they could hear their story, and once again they repeated to me that they were not interested in any of that. And then I brought in the boy who was more open, more social, and he repeated the story. After that, the boy went out and I asked the personnel there to serve some juice to the children and so on, and I went back to the office where there was a discussion with what to do with the children. Based on the conversation with the children, I learned that the children had an uncle and an aunt in Jablanica and they expressed a wish to go to them. I conveyed that to Mr. Sefer Halilovic and to the rest of them, which they categorically refused, asking that the children either be removed or kept at the base until the end of the offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana, I believe that is time for us to break, since we have another sitting using this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just -- I was waiting for the witness just to have said his last sentence. Yes, this is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, we have to break today and I have to remind you that during your stay in The Hague you are under the oath. So do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your evidence. You may have a talk with your counsel concerning the legal issues concerning with your rights as well as other administrative or procedural matters, but do not talk to him about the facts, especially those you are going to give tomorrow and you -- what you have already given today. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
